title: The Nazareth sermon (Luke 4:16–30)
hook: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom to captives

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke's family tree ran back past Abraham to Adam, son of God. Your line was everyone's family. Which stranger did you remember you're related to? Day four hundred fifty-one.

After the desert, Jesus comes back to Galilee, and word about him spreads through the whole region. Then he goes home. Nazareth, where he was brought up. On the Sabbath he goes into the synagogue, as was his custom, Luke says. These are people who watched him grow up. They know his family. He stands up to read, and the attendant hands him the scroll of the prophet Isaias. He unrolls it, and finds the place he's looking for.
screen: `HOME TO NAZARETH.` → `AS WAS HIS CUSTOM.` → `THE SCROLL OF ISAIAS.`

segments.voice: He reads, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." And on: to heal the contrite of heart, to preach deliverance to the captives and sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord. Anointed is the root of the title Christ: Christos, the anointed one, in Hebrew Messiah. And the acceptable year of the Lord echoes the jubilee in the law of Moses, a year when land went back to its families and those sold into service went free. Then he rolls up the scroll, hands it back, and sits down, the posture of a teacher. Every eye in the room is fixed on him. And the sermon Luke gives us is one sentence: "This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears." At first they're impressed; they marvel at his gracious words. Then someone says: isn't this Joseph's son? And Jesus answers that no prophet is accepted in his own country. He reminds them of two old stories we read a few weeks ago: Elias was sent not to the widows of Israel but to a widow in Sarepta of Sidon; Eliseus healed not the lepers of Israel but Naaman the Syrian. God's blessing going to outsiders. The hometown crowd is filled with anger. They drive him out of town to the brow of the hill, to throw him down. But he, passing through the midst of them, went his way. Luke puts this scene near the start of the ministry, and some readers hear it as a program for everything that follows: good news for the poor, and a welcome wider than anyone expected.
screen: `THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD IS UPON ME.` · `ANOINTED: CHRISTOS, MESSIAH.` · `THE ACCEPTABLE YEAR: A JUBILEE.` · `ISN'T THIS JOSEPH'S SON?` · then, large: `THIS DAY IS FULFILLED THIS SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Luke 4:18 aloud. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, find it now, and read the verse out loud, slowly, the way Jesus read it in the synagogue. If you don't, say the phrases after this: good news to the poor. Healing for the brokenhearted. Deliverance to captives. Sight to the blind. Liberty for the bruised. Settle, and breathe. Then let each phrase land on a real person you know: someone poor, someone heartbroken, someone stuck, someone who can't see a way out. If you pray, you can hold each of them before God. The bell holds the time.
Christos. Greek for the anointed one: the title's root, read aloud by Jesus in the Nazareth synagogue the day he said this scripture is fulfilled. Today's word.
Your line: good news to the poor. Today, be good news to one person who's struggling: a meal, a call, an hour of your time. Day four hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 4:16–21 at the Chrism Mass of Holy Week, when the bishop blesses the holy oils, and on a Sunday in Ordinary Time in the year of Luke's Gospel.

original.note: Greek: he has anointed me, Luke 4:18; from chrio, to anoint, the root of Christos, the anointed one.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus read a nice verse in church.
what it means: in his own hometown, Jesus announces his mission from Isaiah, good news for the poor, and is nearly killed for saying God's welcome reaches outsiders.
what a scholar hears: the reading combines Isaiah 61:1–2 with a line from 58:6; the acceptable year recalls the jubilee of Leviticus 25; Luke places it as a programmatic opening.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the invented "bought tables from his father"; corrected the jubilee (Leviticus 25 returns land and frees those sold into service; debt release is the sabbatical year of Deuteronomy 15); "his sermon is one sentence" now "the sermon Luke gives us"; "programmatic" reading attributed to some readers; myth 1 reworded; cut the unsourced "often quoted in social teaching".
Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 4:18 and 4:21 quoted from memory; please check. The rest of 4:18–19 is paraphrased, close to the Douay.
The Douay's 4:19 adds 'and the day of reward' (from the Vulgate); the script doesn't raise the common claim that Jesus stopped before 'the day of vengeance'.
The writer's illustration about buying tables from Joseph was cut in the 2026-10-01 review as invention.
The widow of Sarepta and Naaman were days 409 and 413 ('a few weeks ago'). Confirm phrasing.
Luke 4:16–21 at the Chrism Mass and on the 3rd Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year C: confirm.
The Nazareth crowd is described as 'the hometown crowd'; the script avoids framing it as Jews against Jesus.
